coach.junta: Atlas Freight scoping call with Dana Whitfield (COO)
coach.cuerpo:
## What happened

A 40-minute call to scope the Northbeam pilot. Dana opened with the dispatch backlog: three coordinators re-keying load confirmations from email into the TMS, about 11 hours a week each. At minute 6 you were already describing the agent that would read the confirmations. She stopped you at minute 9: *"Before the how — I need to know what breaks if it's wrong."* You recovered well, but you spent the next ten minutes answering a question you had not asked her.

## What worked

- **You quantified fast.** "Three people, eleven hours each, that's a full headcount a week" landed. She repeated it back to you later, which means it is now her number.
- **You named the owner.** When she asked who answers if the agent mis-keys a rate, you said "your coordinator approves every write for the first 30 days." That is the sentence that kept the call alive.
- **You closed on a date.** Proposal by Friday, decision call the week after. Clean.

## The one thing to change

**Ask the cost question before you pitch.** Dana's role is COO of a freight broker: being wrong on a rate costs her a customer; being right saves her hours nobody thanks her for. Her cost function is asymmetric, and you pitched upside to someone who was listening for downside.

The question you skipped, at minute 5:

> "What's the worst thing that could happen if we automate this and it gets one wrong?"

Her answer would have handed you the pilot's guardrails, and she would have designed half of the proposal for you.

## ✍️ The better line

What you said:
> "So basically the agent reads every confirmation and pushes it straight into the TMS, and your team just stops doing that."

What lands with a COO:
> "For the first month the agent drafts every entry and your coordinator approves it. You see the error rate before anything writes on its own."

Same system. The second version tells her she keeps control, and it gives her a number to watch.

## English

- *"Pushes it straight into"* reads as reckless in a risk conversation. Prefer **"drafts it for approval."**
- You said *"we will guarantee"* twice. In US business English that is a contractual word. Use **"we'll commit to"** or **"the target is."**

## For Friday's proposal

Lead with the approval step and the 30-day error report, not the hours saved. The hours are the reason she'll sign; the control is the reason she'll let you start.

coach.junta: Founders' Table planning with Sofia Herrera
coach.cuerpo:
## What happened

A 25-minute planning session for Saturday's demo night. Agenda: speaker order, the RSVP gap (19 confirmed against the 25+ goal), food budget. You arrived with a finished run of show and walked through it in four minutes. Sofia had a different speaker order in her notes; she didn't bring it up until you asked "anything else?" at the very end.

## What worked

- **The RSVP problem got an owner and a deadline.** "Each of us texts eight people by Thursday night" is concrete, split evenly, and checkable.
- **You cut the budget debate short with a number.** "$14 a head, pizza and one dessert, done." She agreed in one line.

## The one thing to change

**Ask before you decide what lands on someone else.** Speaker order, the MC, and who handles check-in all land on Sofia on Saturday night, not on you. You decided all three. She agreed, but the agreement was thin: her *"sure, that works"* came after a three-second pause both times.

The question to ask the person it lands on:

> "You're the one running the floor Saturday. What order would make your night easier?"

## ✍️ The better line

What you said:
> "Okay so the order is Liam, then the two logistics teams, then Omar closes. I'll MC."

What keeps her in it:
> "Here's a first cut on the order. You know the room better than I do. What would you change?"

Ten more seconds. She brings her notes out, and on Saturday it's her plan too.

## English

- *"Okay so"* opened four of your turns. Once is natural; four times it reads as rushing. Drop it and start with the point.
- Good use of **"let's lock it"** to close a decision. Keep it.

## For tonight

When you text your eight people, send Sofia the draft order with one question: "Swap anything?" That repairs the three decisions without reopening them.

coach.junta: CS 210 project check-in with Prof. Priya Nair
coach.cuerpo:
## What happened

Fifteen minutes at office hours to show the retrieval prototype for your final project. Prof. Nair asked one question twice: *"How do you know it's retrieving the right note and not just a plausible one?"* Both times you answered by showing another feature: the citation link, then the re-ranking step.

## What worked

- **The demo was tight.** Two queries, both answered with sources, under three minutes. She said "that's further along than most," and she doesn't say it often.
- **You admitted the gap once you saw it.** "Honestly I haven't measured that" (cut the *honestly*) was the right move, and her tone changed after it.

## The one thing to change

**When an evaluator repeats a question, the answer is evidence, not capability.** A professor's job is grading what is shown to be true. A new feature tells her what the system *can* do; she asked what it *does* do, on how many cases, with what error.

The sentence that would have ended it in one turn:

> "I haven't measured it yet. My plan is 30 questions with known answers and a hit rate at top-3. Would that satisfy the evaluation section?"

## ✍️ The better line

What you said:
> "So it also re-ranks, so the top one is usually right."

What an evaluator wants:
> "On the ten queries I tried, the right note was first in seven. I'll run thirty before the milestone."

*Usually* is the word that made her ask a second time.

## English

- You used **"basically"** five times in fifteen minutes. In an academic setting it shrinks your claims. Drop it.

## For the milestone (due Nov 3)

Build the 30-question test set this week. It is two hours of work and it is the evaluation section of your report.

borradores.post:
Can you be happy and not know it?

Aristotle would say yes. For him happiness isn't a feeling; it's doing the human thing well, over a whole life. One good day doesn't count.

I've been testing that against my own weeks. The days I'd rate highest aren't the ones I felt best. They're the ones where I did the hard thing I said I'd do.
borradores.huella: - From PHIL 120. 41 reactions, 6 comments; Grace Kim's comment is worth a reply.

borradores.post:
My AI assistant kept telling me my focus was classes. It was October. That note was from August.

The bug wasn't the model. It was memory that never forgot.

What fixed it: every fact that can go stale now carries a date, and a new fact replaces the old one without erasing it. The assistant trusts the newest, and I can still see what changed.

Most "AI memory" problems I've seen are filing problems.

borradores.post:
33 hours a week.

That's how long three coordinators at a small freight broker spend copying load confirmations from email into their system. Same fields, same PDFs, every day.

The first instinct is to automate the copying. The better question is what breaks if the automation gets one wrong. A mis-keyed rate costs a customer. Nobody gets thanked for the hours saved.

So the pilot we're proposing starts the other way around: for 30 days the agent drafts every entry and a coordinator approves it. The client sees the error rate before anything writes on its own.

Speed is the reason they'll sign. Control is the reason they'll let us start.
